topic.name: Council finances
topic.plain_english: Where Norwich City Council's money comes from, what it plans to spend, what it actually spends, and what it owes. It bills you for council tax but keeps only about 13p of every pound: in its own words, "73p going to Norfolk County Council and 14p to the Police and Crime Commissioner". The county's share pays for things like social care and roads. This page is only about the 13p.

questions.asked: Every winter the council asks residents what they think of its budget plans. For 2026/27 it ran a survey from 4 December 2025 to 18 January 2026 and got 899 replies, against a post-2019 average of 1,361. More people opposed the council tax rise than backed it — 48% against, 28% for — and the same survey found 38% unhappy with how the council delivers services against 27% happy. The council published all of it.
questions.decided: Cabinet agreed the budget on 11 February 2026 and full Council set the tax at Budget Council on 24 February. The rise went through at 2.99% — just under the 3% that would have forced a referendum — taking the city's share of a Band D bill to £315.26. Alongside it £313,000 of extra items was put forward, to be paid for from the contingency fund. No minutes of that meeting are in this archive, so we cannot say here how the vote went.
questions.done: Day-to-day spending has come in under budget for five years running, by between 1% and 6.2%. The building programme is a different story: over those same five years the council spent £218.6m of a £342.9m programme, so about a third of the work it approved did not happen in the year it was approved for. Money set aside for emergencies has sat at £8.249m for four year-ends, above the £5.5m floor the council's own finance officer sets.
